title: Two strangers can agree on a secret while everyone listens in
body: Before the 1970s, encrypting a message meant both sides first had to share a secret key. Public-key cryptography broke that rule: you publish a key anyone can use to lock a message, while only your private key can unlock it. It relies on maths that is easy one way and very hard to reverse, such as multiplying two huge primes versus factoring the result. Every HTTPS connection depends on it.

slides.heading: The paint analogy
slides.text: Both sides start with a public colour and each mixes in a secret one. They swap mixes and add their own secret again, ending with the same colour no onlooker can unmix.

slides.heading: Oldest first
items: GCHQ finds the ideas in secret
Diffie and Hellman publish key exchange
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman invent RSA
slides.explanation: GCHQ got there first in the early 1970s but kept it secret; Diffie–Hellman came in 1976, RSA in 1977, and the GCHQ work stayed classified until 1997.

slides.heading: Published in 1976
slides.text: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published their key exchange in 1976. In 1977, Rivest, Shamir and Adleman invented RSA, which also handles digital signatures.

slides.heading: The secret twist
slides.text: At Britain’s GCHQ, James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson had found the same ideas in the early 1970s, but their work stayed classified until 1997.
